title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ πάρδαλις
part: The Fox and the Leopard (Chambry 37 · Perry 12)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 37 (= Perry 12). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ πάρδαλις περὶ κάλλους ἤριζον.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx kai pardalis peri kallous ērizon.
sentences.l: A fox and a leopard were quarrelling about beauty.
sentences.n: πάρδαλις is the spotted cat, leopard or panther; the spots are the whole point of the argument.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ παρδάλεως παρ’ ἕκαστα τὴν τοῦ σώματος ποικιλίαν προβαλλομένης, ἡ ἀλώπηξ ὑποτυχοῦσα ἔφη· « Καὶ πόσον ἐγὼ σοῦ καλλίων ὑπάρχω, ἥτις οὐ τὸ σῶμα, τὴν δὲ ψύχην πεποίκιλμαι. »
sentences.tr: Tēs de pardaleōs par’ hekasta tēn tou sōmatos poikilian proballomenēs, hē alōpēx hypotychousa ephē· « Kai poson egō sou kalliōn hyparchō, hētis ou to sōma, tēn de psychēn pepoikilmai. »
sentences.l: And the leopard at every point putting forward the dappling of her body, the fox, taking her up, said: « And how much fairer am I than you, I who have been dappled not in body, but in soul. »
sentences.i: At every turn the leopard paraded the dappling of her coat; and the fox broke in and said, “How much fairer am I than you — I who am dappled not in body but in soul!”
sentences.n: The exchange rests on a single word doing two jobs: ποικίλος and its family mean “dappled, many-coloured” and equally “subtle, versatile, wily.” The leopard means her coat; the fox means her wits. τὸ σῶμα and τὴν ψυχήν are accusatives of respect with the perfect πεποίκιλμαι — “dappled as to the body… as to the soul.” ὑποτυχοῦσα, “having taken up (the word),” is this collection's standing phrase for cutting in with a reply. The accusative is printed here as ψύχην; the word is ψυχή, whose accusative is ψυχήν, and the accent as it stands is anomalous.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι τοῦ σωματικοῦ κάλλους ἀμείνων ἐστὶν ὁ τῆς διανοίας κόσμος.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti tou sōmatikou kallous ameinōn estin ho tēs dianoias kosmos.
sentences.l: The story shows that better than beauty of the body is the adornment of the mind.
sentences.i: The story shows that the adornment of the mind is better than beauty of the body.
sentences.n: ἀμείνων, a comparative, takes the genitive of comparison (τοῦ σωματικοῦ κάλλους) where English needs “than.” κόσμος is “ordered arrangement” and so “ornament” — the same word that later means the ordered universe.
